n: Elisha sends a young prophet to Ramoth-gilead, where Israel’s army is stationed, with a flask of anointing oil. This carries out the last of the three commissions given to Elijah at Horeb.

f.g: a flask or vial of olive oil for anointing.

n: He is to find Jehu, an army commander, and take him privately into an inner room.

f.g: ‘Jehovah is He’; not the prophet Jehu son of Hanani.

n: He must anoint Jehu as king, declare the Lord’s word, and run. Anointing with oil symbolized being chosen and empowered by God.
The young prophet goes to Ramoth-gilead.
He finds the officers in council and says he has a message for “the commander.” Jehu asks which one; he answers, “For you.”
Inside, he pours the oil on Jehu’s head and declares him king over “the people of the LORD.”
Jehu is commissioned to strike down Ahab’s house, avenging the blood of the prophets Jezebel killed.

f.w: avenge the blood of my servants the prophets

n: Every male of Ahab’s line will be cut off, as Elijah prophesied.

f.w: him that pisseth against the wall
f.g: a crude idiom for every male.

n: Ahab’s house will end like the dynasties of Jeroboam and Baasha.
Jezebel will be eaten by dogs at Jezreel, unburied. Then the young prophet runs off.

f.g: in the territory or plot of land at Jezreel.

n: The officers ask why this “madman” came. Prophets’ unusual behavior sometimes earned them that label. Jehu tries to brush it off.

f.g: a crazy man; a scornful term for prophets.

n: They don’t buy it—“That’s a lie, tell us!” Jehu admits that he has been anointed king.
The officers immediately spread their cloaks on the steps as a makeshift throne carpet, blow trumpets, and proclaim, “Jehu is king!”
Jehu begins his coup against King Joram, whose army had been holding Ramoth-gilead against Hazael.
Joram had gone to Jezreel to recover from his wounds. Jehu orders that no one leave the city to warn him.
Jehu races to Jezreel, where both Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of Judah are staying.
A watchman on Jezreel’s tower sees Jehu’s troops approaching. Joram sends a rider to ask, “Is it peace?”—that is, is all well?

f.g: Hebrew hashalom: ‘Is all well?’ ‘Do you come in peace?’

n: Jehu tells the rider, “What do you care about peace? Fall in behind me.” The messenger doesn’t return.
A second rider meets the same fate.
The watchman recognizes Jehu by his reckless, furious driving. The phrase became proverbial.
Joram and Ahaziah ride out in their chariots to meet Jehu—and they meet at Naboth’s field, the very land Ahab stole. The setting is no coincidence.

f.w: the portion of Naboth the Jezreelite

n: Joram asks, “Is it peace?” Jehu answers that there can be no peace while Jezebel’s idolatry and sorcery continue. “Whoredoms” is the prophets’ image for spiritual unfaithfulness to God.
Joram turns his chariot and flees, crying, “Treachery!”
Jehu draws his bow with full force and shoots Joram through the back, piercing his heart.
Jehu orders Joram’s body thrown on Naboth’s plot. He recalls riding with Bidkar behind Ahab when the Lord pronounced this “burden”—the prophecy of judgment.

f.g: an oracle, a weighty prophetic pronouncement.

n: Jehu quotes the Lord: He saw Naboth’s blood and his sons’ blood, and would repay it on that very plot. This adds that Naboth’s sons were also murdered.
Ahaziah of Judah flees south, but Jehu’s men wound him near Ibleam. He reaches Megiddo and dies. Chronicles gives a slightly different account of his death.

f.w: he fled to Megiddo, and died there

n: His servants bring his body to Jerusalem for burial in the royal tombs.
A note on chronology: Ahaziah began to reign in Joram’s eleventh year (8:25 says twelfth—the difference likely reflects different ways of counting years).
Jezebel, hearing Jehu is coming, puts on eye makeup and arranges her hair, then looks out a window. She meets death with royal defiance.

f.g: lined her eyes with dark cosmetic (kohl).

n: She taunts him by calling him “Zimri,” the traitor who killed his king and lasted only seven days.
Jehu calls out, “Who is on my side?” Two or three palace eunuchs look down.

f.g: court officials, often castrated servants of the royal household.

n: At his command they throw her down. Her blood splatters the wall and horses, and Jehu drives over her.
Jehu eats and drinks, then orders her burial out of respect for her royal birth as daughter of Sidon’s king.
Only her skull, feet, and hands remain; the dogs have devoured the rest.
Jehu recognizes the fulfillment of Elijah’s prophecy word for word.

f.w: In the portion of Jezreel shall dogs eat the flesh of Jezebel

n: Jezebel’s remains become like refuse on the field, without even a grave to bear her name. The queen who opposed the Lord’s prophets ends forgotten, as God’s word declared.
